utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend Mr. Zecevic just told me that in the previous document which is under the number P2113 he found one mistake, so I would like to ask my learned friend to clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, just for the sake of clarity, according to the Serbian text paragraph 2 it says: "It is approved by the commands of MUP and VJ ..." And in the English text it says: "Command of the MUP and the Yugoslav Army ..." I believe the distinction is -- because there is obviously in the Serbian original it refers to more commands, so the MUP and the VJ as a separate entities and separate commands. According to the English text, it might be understood as one command which compromises [sic] MUP and the VJ. And the Serbian text clearly says "K/DE," [B/C/S spoken] meaning plural. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Please proceed, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is Slup and Voksa. You've seen the order twice already. Can we please have Defence Exhibit 5D1175. General, sir, do you see this decision map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who signed it and who approved it, this decision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approved by the 3rd Army commander. At the time this was Lieutenant-General Dusan Samardzic, and it was signed by the Pristina Corps commander, General Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Now 5D1174, can we have that called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but I really can't say. This is a forward command post of the 3rd Army after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 in the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You see the date on that document, the 14th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... third page, count 5 I need. Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please look at BG-15-3 support MUP forces. Are these all the same places? I hereby decide, is that something to do with the map, the decision map that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, or rather, can we please go to the last page of the Serbian text, the B/C/S, to see who signed this document and who took the decision. You recognise these names, sir, don't you, the ones who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. You can tell that the decision was taken by Colonel-General Dusan Samardzic, and then it reads: "The telegram may be sent ..." This is signed and stamped by the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-General Miodrag Simic. This is a document that was dispatched by the forward command post of the 3rd Army based in the Kosovo Heroes Barracks in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Just one last question about this topic. Is this a regular chain of command? Is this a document that was produced by a regular army procedure or is this some sort of a Joint Command or some third party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the most regular procedure possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can we please have P2023. Before that document appears I would like to say that my learned friend Mr. Ivetic asked you a number of questions too. Also when this document was on the screen, he read this document back to you and he asked you questions about this. The forces of the 73rd MUP Detachment were under your command. And if you look at item 2 where it says Rugovska Klisura and then just underneath.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. My question is: What about those forces? Were they at any point resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that is a result of inertia, if you like. It was drafted by default and based on a Pristina Corps command on the resubordination of MUP units to a combined arms tactical units. These forces were not in actual fact resubordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Mr. Ivetic was asking a number of questions and making several references to your zone, inside your zone. So this zone what I want to know about who is in charge of public order and the safety of persons and property in this zone, and what are the duties of the army in these terms inside their zone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Zone" is a very broad concept. You organize positions and sectors for defence inside a zone. The military are responsible for the situation in those sectors, and the sectors are a much narrower concept than a zone. All the main areas and especially all the principal roads in Kosovo and Metohija during the war were under the authority of civilian bodies or bodies of local self government and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can we please now have a document that Mr. Ivetic showed you yesterday, I'm talking about Exhibit 5D794. Since this was not a document that was produced by the 125th Brigade, I will be asking you to read it in full, please. Maybe we should scroll the document further down, so please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many pages are there on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think three, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is it necessary for the witness to read it all in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to ask because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got as far as "intelligence support." I think I get the gist of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please allow Mr. Cepic to tell me why this needs to be read in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just in order to clarify what Mr. Ivetic asked yesterday about this document and the possibility of resubordinating MUP units to forces of the VJ, and this witness was not given a chance to see the entire document although he was, in fact, asked questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you unhappy with the answers to these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would require some clarification, just for the sake of completeness. [In English] Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, you've had a look. Can you tell me who this order is being issued to based on the face of this document. Is it to some police forces, just to speed things up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by the commander of the 7th Infantry Brigade being issued to his own units, an order; and he's talking about his neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is there any sort of task that is being handed out to the 125th Brigade or police units or any other unit in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not possible for the commander of the 7th Brigade to hand out any assignments to units of the 125th Brigade. This is not something that had been agreed upon and there is no original document produced by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether in this document any assignments are given to units of the 125th or to police units. Now, does the document bear to give any such tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the answer to the question you were asked was quite different, and we know that you've claimed repeatedly that the commander of one brigade can't order other soldiers who are not resubordinated to him or order members of the MUP. We've heard this repeatedly in this court, but then when you look at the documents they appear to say other things, Mr. Cepic. Now why you think re-examination is going to help resolve this I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I understand, at least when I read this document, no assignments were handed out to the 125th Brigade or the PJP units. It just says, Support the actions of these two units, that's 5.1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're unhappy with the answer that Mr. Zivanovic gave to my question, then you have to explore it further because he said that there are tasks given to these bodies on the face of the document. You can make your own submissions at the end of the case. If you want any more from him, then ask him the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what about this order, this document that you have in front of you, do we see any sort of assignment being handed out in it to the 125th Brigade or any of the PJP units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document anticipates what some elements of the 125th Brigade and the PJP should do, but this was never elaborated on, at least not as far as my armoured battalion was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. General, you mentioned about 1998, the summer of 1998, that you received several orders from the Chief of the General Staff. Just for the sake of clarity, who was at the time the Chief of the General Staff and who did you receive that from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it orally through our communications equipment. The person in question was Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit P3049. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, my learned friend Mr. Hannis showed you this order dated the 19th of March, 1999. So can we have item 10 of this order, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have back page in English and the last page in B/C/S, please. Count 10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, what is item 10 in reference to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about command and communications, as per usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what does this abbreviation mean, "KM PrK in peacetime location.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means Pristina Corps command post at its peacetime location which means its usual building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is that where command was exercised from as reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P1967 now. Thank you. Last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, just to speed things up a little, you saw this document during the cross-examination by Mr. Hannis. Do you think we should go through it to see what the units were, all of them who were handed out assignments or do you perhaps remember this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the 125th in part and the 354th Brigades were involved for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Look at this last sentence here: "Command post in the Lausa sector." Have you ever been to that location, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the command post of the 354th Brigade in the village of Lausa. I've never been there myself. This is Lausa and it's in Malo Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was this perhaps the command post for all the forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That's a blatantly leading question in the middle of re-examination, Mr. Cepic. Please confine yourself to open questions at this stage. It's now doubtful whether the answer that will be given will be of any value to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you perhaps know whether the entire area in which these activities by units took place can actually be seen or taken in from that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were I to be shown a map perhaps I could provide that answer. Since, as I said, I've never been there, I can hardly say, can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you were shown a document by my colleague Mr. Hannis, it's P1246. While we are waiting for the document to come up on the screen, when replying to his question you spoke about the carrying out of the concept of All People's Defence and social self defense when explaining the document in connection with sanitization. Here it is now. General, you said from when this concept was in force this idea of All People's Defence and social self defence, was it carried out in practice later on in -- after -- in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Who was exercising power on the territory and who was authorised on the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime it was the organs of local self management and other organs whose duty it was to ensure public law and order, that is the units and secretariats of the MUP, or rather, the judiciary as well, the prosecutor's office, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honour, just to check my drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have no further questions for you. That was my last question. Thank you for your responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence again. You, no doubt, hope that's the end of the road as far as you're concerned. I can give you no guarantees, but perhaps it is. Anyway, you're now free to leave the courtroom with our thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Our next witness is Colonel Milan Kotus.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kotur, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If I may ask the usher to lower the ELMO because it's in the way, it's obstructing communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please be so kind as to state for the record your name and your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: My name is Milan Kotur I was born on the 23rd of September, 1947, in Indjija. That's a northern province in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us briefly what your education is and something about your career.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I completed the highest military schools, and as for my career I served in ten garrisons, Samobor, Zagreb, Varazdin, Koprivnica, Leskovac, Kursumlija, Kosovska Mitrovica, Pristina, Leskovac, and Novi Sad. And then I retired with a rank of colonel. I'm now retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kotur. Tell us, what were your main duties in the Army of Yugoslavia in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I was the chief of infantry in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you the chief of infantry throughout 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In what garrison were you and where were you quartered when in 1998 you performed this duty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I was quartered in the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until what date? Did you leave Pristina to go somewhere else; and if you did, where and why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: In 1998, we went to Djakovica to the forward command post, where we stayed sometime until the 23rd of October of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You are speaking in the plural, but I asked you about your yourself. So who did you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I was referring to the forward command post command where most of the officers headed by Colonel Lazarevic were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when did this forward command post begin functioning and until when were you there at that command post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, in late April 1998, that's when it started functioning, and I remained at that forward command post until the 23rd of October of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, 1998, did you take on any other duty and what did you do from that point on if you did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: As of the 23rd of October I still remained chief of infantry in the Pristina Corps, but in addition to this, I also performed the duty of team leader in the Pristina Corps for relations with the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's late in the day and it's Friday. The interpreters are managing to catch up, but could you please make a break between question and answer, a brief pause. When you became a team member for cooperation with the OSCE mission, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: When I became team leader for relations with the Kosovo Verification Mission on behalf of the Pristina Corps, I was stationed in the Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until what date were you in the team for cooperation with the OSCE -- well, first of all, let me ask you this: Until when were you team leader of the Pristina Corps for cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I was the team leader of the Pristina Corps for cooperation with the Kosovo Verification Mission until the 10th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After this date did you continue being a member of the team for cooperation with the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I remained in the mixed team which was created for relations with the Kosovo Verification Mission after the 10th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, we will go through some documents now, and we'll come to this topic in greater detail. Before we begin looking at documents, could you, if you can, describe in general the relationship of representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Kosovo Verification Mission. What was the attitude of the Pristina Corps, to put it more precisely, towards the Kosovo Verification Mission in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The Kosovo Verification Mission was formed pursuant to the approval inter alia of the federal government, and the body had diplomatic status. All the members of that mission had protected diplomatic status. Our attitude toward that mission was one of respect, it was very correct, and it was our desire and intention for the problem of Kosovo and Metohija to be resolved by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, could we now take a look at an exhibit, our time is limited, and I have selected several documents from which we shall be able to see what your attitude toward the mission was and vice versa. We'll try to depict this for the Trial Chamber. So I'll draw your attention now to a document referring to an incident which was referred to in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 5D1387 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, please look at item in B/C/S. It's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Tell me, please, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Under 3 it says: "C." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That is a verifier, Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain what this is about, what the gist of this paragraph is to avoid reading it out loud. We can all read it for ourselves, but just tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, according to a report from the Siptar terrorist army and the media in Kosovo and Metohija, Ivaja and the villages around it were alleged to be a ghost town or ghost village which had been burnt to the ground and everybody there killed, that it was all looted, and that all this was done by it Serbian forces. Colonel Ciaglinski here is informing me that General DZ was Mr. Walker's operations assistant had been in Kacanik and Ivaja and established that there had been fighting there, that there was shooting, and that some houses were damaged, but there was no plundering. Instead, certain houses were searched, and he considered this to be normal procedure. Therefore, the situation is not even remotely such as described, so there is a witness on the ground who can refute the KLA allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kotur. You testified in another case here in this Tribunal. I think that a report was shown to you from a blue book and it seemed that there had been a suggestion that this report from the federal ministry had been doctored or was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we now look at an OSCE working document. It's a Prosecution exhibit, 5680 [as interpreted]. It's a working document for the period from the 26th of February to the 4th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the transcript I see the number is referred to as 5680. That's not a Prosecution exhibit number. Maybe it was misspoken or mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P680. It seems the interpreters were correct, but the transcript may contain a typographical error. The document we see is the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, to expedite matters, on the first page where it says KLA and Djeneral Jankovic, it says in the OSCE report that: "It would seem that over a hundred KLA members crossed the border and combined with the said militia while encouraging the locals to leave."

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's towards the bottom of the page, could we scroll down a bit, in B/C/S and let's move to page 2 of this document. Look at paragraph 1 where it says: "Euronews reported that a Serb offensive had started, this was accompanied by images of Serbian vehicles on the move and local people with sad expressions on their faces. The village of Kacanik has been described as a ghost town, whereas the verifiers have stated this was untrue and the first reports coming from the region seem to imply that there had been a massacre." This working document of the OSCE, does this correspond with what we saw in the previous report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond with what Mr. Ciaglinski told me and what is contained in the previous report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, no, no. I may have mistaken the paragraph. Paragraphs I was looking at the wrong paragraph. Oh yes, all right, all right, now I see it. No, no I was right. It says that it's untrue that it was a ghost town. I wasn't sure I had read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at the last paragraph on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just scroll down a little bit, please, in order for the last paragraph in B/C/S to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see here some activities of the KLA in the Podujevo area. Can you comment on that, please, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: KLA forces in the Podujevo area succeeded in launching an attack in the town itself successfully winning over the Serbs, unlike only reactions and defence as previously while they killed the Serbs there to the last man. They killed two people going to work in the town of Podujevo. They were not inactive. They didn't react only when they were attacked. It wasn't just a response to an attack. That's what's referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, what is suggested here is that the VJ was only responding to attacks and defending itself.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: They say: "Unlike merely responding and defending themselves they also attacked and killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia responded only when it was provoked or attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, can we now move to page 4 where there is a paragraph concerning the Army of Yugoslavia. Let's look at the last paragraph where it says "VJ," Army of Yugoslavia. In this paragraph it says: "The forces of the VJ in Kosovo have strengthened their training" --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Can we zoom in, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Have significantly stepped-up their training on the territory of the entire region, and although there are more VJ troops on the ground than after the October agreement, estimates speak of 15 combat teams. Their actions are minimalist and this can only be compared with the KLA provocations, possibly a reflection of the KLA activity." It seems that the army's actions are minimalist, that the army was simply responding to KLA provocations. But please tell us whether there actually were 15 combat teams deployed there who were beyond the scope of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, there were never 15 teams deployed that were not part of the agreement in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we now move on to another document now that we're discussing this topic and then we'll come back briefly to this exhibit. Could we now take a look at Prosecution Exhibit P2772, MM9, that's a sketch of these 15 teams, or rather, combat groups allegedly deployed in the area outside the scope of the agreement. And as team leader, could you please describe this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I still don't have that on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's about to come up. Just a minute, please. This is MM9 and the page number is 20075691. In e-court it's page 85, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn this around, please, and zoom in slightly so that we see the entire map on our screens. The left-hand page is irrelevant. Please zoom in just slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, can you comment, please. Start with the square on the right-hand side where it says Stimlje and take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Under the agreement on Kosovo and Metohija, the Pristina Corps was allowed to have three groups across the area, and these groups were in Stimlje and Dulje. That was one group in two different locations. The other group was in the Volujak area. And the third group was in the Lapusnik area, or rather, the rear of that group was in Komorane, it was also one and the same group in two different locations. So these were the three combat groups that were allowed to be in the area under the verification agreement. Under the verification agreement, all combat groups that were within the border belt protecting the state border remained and were not subject to this verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me interrupt you there for a second. Can you please notice or can you tell us how many points there are on this sketch that refer to what you have been telling us about, the combat groups that were securing the state border and were within the border belt which was not contrary to the terms of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I'll tell you about what's outside the agreement and everything else was under the agreement. That is the easier approach. The group that was not within the agreement was the group at Vucitrn. The next group, Podujevo. I don't know about Bajgora. We didn't have a group over there. I'm not sure what it is that's marked. I think - I'm looking at the location - it could be a firing range, Crnusak [phoen] right next to Kosovska Mitrovica. If you take into account the firing range, Kosovska Mitrovica, Bajgora, Vucitrn, and Podujevo. Podujevo, well, this is probably the Slatina airport if that's what's drawn here, but I can't see, I can't know for sure. So those are the three groups that are marked here that were outside the agreement in a manner of speaking and everything else was perfectly in keeping with the terms of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Those in keeping with the agreement, securing the state border, can you explain how these three groups were there that were not in keeping with the terms of the October agreement. Were they outside the agreement or is it just that the agreement did not envisage them to be there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: They weren't envisaged in the agreement, but we have a number of memoranda, whatever they were called at the time, and one of these documents says that we in case of danger, danger to our country or in order to protect our roads, were allowed the right to react. What I see here, the 10th of March, 2000, the year is 2000, I'm not sure if that's the date when the groups were there or it's something else because I see a stamp there. If indeed it's the 10th of March, 2000 -- it can't be 2000, can it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please pay that no heed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to know on which date this disposition of groups was represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I think in February, February or March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: In February and March 1999 the situation in Kosovo and Metohija became more complex. Given what the situation was, the operative situation of the Pristina Corps, our conclusion was that we were facing odds that weren't favourable at all and this was one of the reasons that we received -- that we admitted several thousands of young and insufficiently trained soldiers. They had not been sufficiently trained because their training programme was no more than two and a half months long and these soldiers were not sufficiently trained to perform their basic military specialty. We had to take them outside the barracks in order to train them. The training proceeded in the following way: There was a combat group that was in the area, and this occurred at the Batlava airport, which is an airfield that was used for flying amateur planes. This is an area that was used every year, and every year in this area we trained men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's try to hurry things a long a little bit. Tell me about Vucitrn, is something, a place called Bukos there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So what was that, can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Bukos is where a group went in order to be trained, a group of young soldiers, likewise and the Crnusak firing range where they had their practice. I see that one of the barracks in Djakovica was marked here, this is no combat group, it's the Djakovica barracks. There are two barracks -- rather, the Djakovica garrison has two different barracks locations. One of them is in the town itself in Djakovica and the other is to the west of the town. I see that the one in the actual town was shown as a combat group, but that is not consistent with the actual situation. So the sketch is erroneous in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct of what you're suggesting, sir, as for those that were outside the agreement we have these three locations with three training grounds, if you like. Under the agreement were you entitled to perform training and drills at these locations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, and the members of the verification mission -- yes, we did have the right and the members of the verification mission said this was a very normal thing for us to do and anything else we might have done in February and March at that time would have been abnormal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's go back to P680 briefly. And thank you very much for your previous answer, Colonel. Page 5 in the B/C/S. Colonel, sir, we see an incident discussed here along the border --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Can we just zoom in slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This was something that was experienced by the OSCE mission. It was the SRJ customs that held them back at the Djeneral Jankovic border post.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I see that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about the customs office, do those people over there have anything to do with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, nothing whatsoever. There was not a single border crossing where there were customs offices and the military too. There were just the customs office and the police, but no military whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the lower half of the page it says that it had been agreed for the border post chief to be replaced. What about the border post, does that have anything to do with the customs people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, nothing whatsoever. The border post is a place where soldiers securing the border post are put up. This is nothing to do with the customs people, not the actual persons who are there nor the installation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know what the proposal was for, who was to be replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: A reference there to Mihalj Kertes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just looking. A meeting between General DZ and General Loncar has cleared the air of the event, although this is not to say that the issue will not occur again. It is agreed that the chief of the border post has been replaced. This is nonsense. There was no agreement nor could there have been an agreement for the border post chief to be dismissed, only the customs chief. This was a nationwide change in attitude and not confined to Djeneral Jankovic and certainly [indiscernible] we will not have changed his opinion, and so on and so forth. I think if this had been agreed for the replacement of the border post chief, I think this is entirely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What was Kertes' position at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: He was a manager -- the manager or whatever it was called at the time of the federal customs in the country at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have this section entitled: "Summary of events prior to the 28th of February." It's about the fact that it seemed that the KLA had entered the area on a large scale, they had joined up with the police. There were between 120 and 160 men involved, the locals heard shooting from the village of Stremce, and this village was nearly and entirely sealed off because of heavy snow fall. The KLA told those living in the area to move out. Are you familiar with this particular piece of information in relation to this area and do you have any information about any other areas.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This is one of the areas in which the KLA ordered their own population to leave in order to give rise to some sort of a humanitarian disaster, in order to end the world's pity and sympathy. It's clear enough if you look at the conversation that took place between Ciaglinski and myself and the book that you mentioned. You can tell that this was one of the methods they employed, and what they wrote there was actually what they succeeded in and that was their chief motive. They wanted to do just that, they wanted to apply these methods and this doesn't just apply to Kacanik, it applied throughout Kosovo. They did this wherever they thought they could get away with that, and whatever they thought they stood to profit from the use of these methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's wrap up this document because we're nearing the end of the day. The very end of this document, sir, page 7 where it reads: "Assessment of the OSCE mission" and then just underneath: "The KLA are exploiting the media." I will read a portion of this to you. Please just comment whether you had this sort of information --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move the page up in the B/C/S so that the witness is able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Knowing the power of the media, the ethnic Albanians will work towards their own good and will do everything they can to get the world's sympathy. The poor situation of internally displaced persons remains their most power weapon. Therefore, one can only expect other things to start happening in relation to the movement -- the large-scale movement of people. Each scenario must be studied and" --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Please pull up the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is paragraph 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you see that now, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please. Can the speakers please be asked to not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, there's no interruption between question and answer here. You really have to not speak at the same time as Mr. Kotur. Now, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that the witness got a different page altogether, but we're passed the mark in terms of time already, and I believe we can press on next Monday with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Complete what you're going to do with this document. You're at --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7, please, in the B/C/S. I see that in the English we have the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please look at where it says: "Assessment," the last paragraph underneath, yes, that's right, the bottom of the page. Further down, please just a little in the B/C/S. You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I read the document. What about this assessment of the OSCE mission, were you familiar with this at the time and did you have the same information at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This appears to be our assessment, not theirs, but they didn't share this with us, they didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, this is an OSCE document and you're being asked whether you -- your experience was consistent with what's being assessed by them that the Albanians would exploit the media to their advantage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that. That was my assessment too. That was our assessment too, such as the one reflected here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a convenient time for us to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you finished with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, I know that you've not been with us for long, but now is the deadline for these proceedings today and we must bring them to an end until next week. That means that you have to return to continue to give evidence on Monday. We have restored the original arrangement for Monday so that we will be sitting at 9.00 in this courtroom and be sitting from 9.00 until 3.30. It's important that between now and then you have no communication with anyone about any aspect of the evidence in this case. Your communications with other people are unlimited so far as other matters are concerned, but absolutely off limits is any communication with anyone else about any aspect of all of the evidence in this case. So please bear that in mind and comply with that direction over the weekend, make the most of the weekend, and return here refreshed, ready to resume your evidence at 9.00 on Monday. Meanwhile, please leave the courtroom with the usher. We're adjourned now until Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not getting any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it should have been intimated to you. It definitely has been changed to 9.00 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
